For a dense subset of values $T \in [T_0,\infty)$, there exists $\varepsilon(T) > 0$ such that for all $\varepsilon \in (0,\varepsilon(T))$, the conically singular harmonic map $\phi \colon \thinspace (\mathbb{CP}^2, g_{\varepsilon,T}) \to (\mathbb{CP}^1, g_{\mathrm{FS}})$ satisfies the assumptions of \cref{thm: main theorem introduction} with respect to the metric $g_{\varepsilon,T} \coloneqq \mathrm{d} t^2 + \mathrm{e}^{2\kappa_{+,T}(t)} \widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon,T}(t)$ on $\mathbb{CP}^2$.
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- prop-25: body_md -->
Suppose that $m = \dim(M) \geq 3$, and let $\phi \colon \thinspace M \backslash S \rightarrow N$ be a conically singular map. Then $\phi \in W^{1,2}(M,N)$.
<!-- end prop-25 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Let us fix an adapted set of charts $\{\Upsilon_s \colon \thinspace \mathbb{B}_R \to M\}$, and identify the maps $\phi \colon \thinspace M \setminus S \to N$ and $\iota \circ \phi \colon \thinspace M \setminus S \to \iota(N) \subset \mathbb{R}^K$. Thus for any $s \in S$, $\phi \circ \Upsilon_s = \phi_s + u_s$ where $\phi_s = \varphi_s(x/|x|)$ for a smooth map $\varphi_s \colon \thinspace \mathbb{S}^{m-1} \to \iota(N)$ and $u_s$ satisfies $|\partial^a u_s| = \mathcal{O}(r^{\mu-|a|})$ for any multi-index $a = (a_1,\ldots,a_m)$.
    
    Since $N$ is compact, the map $\phi \colon \thinspace M \setminus S \rightarrow \iota(N) \subset \mathbb{R}^K$ is bounded and thus $\phi \in L^2(M,N)$. Moreover, for any $s \in S$ and $j = 1,\ldots, m$, $|\partial_{x_j}(\phi \circ \Upsilon_s)| = \mathcal{O}(r^{-1})$ since $|\partial_{x_j} \phi_s| = \mathcal{O}(r^{-1})$ and $|\partial_{x_j} u_s | = \mathcal{O}(r^{\mu-1})$. Since $m \geq 3$, it follows that $\mathrm{d}\phi_{|M \setminus S}$ is $L^2$. It remains to see that $\mathrm{d}\phi_{|M\setminus S}$ coincides with the weak (distributional) derivative of $\phi$. Since $\phi$ is smooth outside of $S$, this amounts to checking that for any $\mathbb{R}^K$-valued function $v \colon \thinspace \mathbb{B}_R \to \mathbb{R}^m$ supported in the interior of $\mathbb{B}_R$, any $s \in S$ and any $1 \leq j \leq K$, 
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_{\mathbb{B}_R} \langle \nabla(\phi^j_s + u^j_s), v \rangle \mathrm{d} x = - \int_{\mathbb{B}_R}  (\phi^j_s + u^j_s) \operatorname{div}(v) \mathrm{d} x
    \end{equation*}
    where the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is taken with respect to the standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^m$, $\nabla$ is the Euclidean gradient and $\operatorname{div}(v)$ the Euclidean divergence. Note that the integrands on both sides of the equality are $L^1$, and therefore these are definite integrals. Using the divergence theorem, we obtain
    \begin{align*}
        \int_{\mathbb{B}_R} \langle \nabla(\phi^j_s + u^j_s), v \rangle \mathrm{d} x & = \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \int_{\mathbb{B}_R \setminus \mathbb{B}_\varepsilon} \langle \nabla(\phi^j_s + u^j_s), v \rangle \mathrm{d} x \\
        & = \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} - \int_{\mathbb{B}_R \setminus \mathbb{B}_\varepsilon}  (\phi^j_s + u^j_s) \operatorname{div}(v) \mathrm{d} x + \int_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon} (\phi^j_s + u^j_s) \langle v, \nu_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon} \rangle \operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon} \\
        & = - \int_{\mathbb{B}_R}  (\phi^j_s + u^j_s) \operatorname{div}(v) \mathrm{d} x + \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon} (\phi^j_s + u^j_s) \langle v, \nu_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon} \rangle \operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon}
    \end{align*}
    where $\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon = \partial \mathbb{B}_\varepsilon$ is the Euclidean sphere of radius $\varepsilon$, $\operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon}$ its standard volume form and $\nu_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon}$ the outwards pointing normal. Since $\phi^j_s + u^j_s$ and $\langle v , \nu_{\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon} \rangle$ are uniformly bounded functions and $\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb{S}^{m-1}_\varepsilon) \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, this proves our claim.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- prop-26: body_md -->
\label{lem: m geq 3}
    Suppose that $m = \dim(M) \geq 3$ and let $\phi \colon \thinspace M \setminus S \to N$ be a map with conical singularities. Then $\phi$ is weakly harmonic if and only if the tension $\tau(\phi)$ on $M \setminus S$.
<!-- end prop-26 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
If $\phi$ is weakly harmonic, the tension field $\tau(\phi)$ must vanish away from the singular locus. To prove the converse statement, remark that since $\phi$ is smooth and harmonic outside of the singular locus $S$, and $\phi \in W^{1,2}(M,N)$ globally, it is enough to prove that the Laplacian $\Delta_g \phi$ (seen as an $\mathbb{R}^K$-valued disribution on $M$) is $L^1$. Outside of $S$, $\Delta_g \phi = \operatorname{tr}_{g} \mathrm{I\!I}_{\phi}(\mathrm{d}\phi,\mathrm{d}\phi)$ so that the function $|\Delta_g \phi|$ is $L^1$ on $M \setminus S$. Therefore it only remains to check for any smooth map $u \colon \thinspace M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$ supported inside a small geodesic ball $B_\delta(s)$ centred at $s \in S$, the following identity holds
    \begin{equation*}
        \int_{B_\delta(s)} \langle \mathrm{d}\phi, \mathrm{d} u \rangle_{g,g_{\mathbb{R}^K}} \operatorname{vol}_{g} = \int_{B_\delta(s) \setminus \{s\}} \langle \Delta_g \phi, u \rangle_{g_{\mathbb{R}^K}} \operatorname{vol}_{g} .
    \end{equation*}
    As in the previous proof, since the integrands on both sides are $L^1$ we can integrate by parts and this boils down to proving that $\lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(s)} u^j (*_{g}\mathrm{d}\phi^j)= 0$ (where we take coordinates $\{y^j\}_{j=1,\ldots,K}$ on $\mathbb{R}^K$). This identity holds since $|\mathrm{d}\phi^j|= \mathcal{O}(r^{-1})$ near $s$ ($r$ being the distance to $s$), and $m-1 \geq 2$ so that the volume of $\partial B_\varepsilon(s)$ behaves as $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{m-1}) \leq \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- lem-40: body_md -->
\label{lem: m geq 4}
    Suppose that $m = \dim(M) \geq 4$. Then any conically singular map $\phi \colon \thinspace M \setminus S \to N$ which is weakly harmonic is stationary.
<!-- end lem-40 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Since $\phi$ is weakly harmonic, stationarity is equivalent to the property that the tensor $T = \tfrac{1}{2} |\mathrm{d}\phi|^2_{g,h} g - \phi^*h$ (which is in $L^1(\mathrm{Sym}^2T^*M)$) be covariantly divergence-free, in the distributional sense (c.f. \cite[\S3.1]{helein2007harmonic} for instance). This property holds outside of $S$ since $\phi$ is smooth on $M \setminus S$. On the other hand, in local adapted coordinates the tensor $T$ takes the form
    \begin{equation*}
        T_{ab} = \frac{1}{2} g^{k\ell} \langle \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x^k}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x^\ell} \rangle g_{ab} - \langle \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x^a}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x^b} \rangle
    \end{equation*}
    where the brackets $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ are defined with respect to the standard inner product of $\mathbb{R}^K$, using the isometric embedding $\iota \colon \thinspace N \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$. This expression shows that $|T|_{g,g_{\mathbb{R}^K}} = \mathcal{O}(r^{-2})$ and $|\nabla T|_{g,g_{\mathbb{R}^K}} = \mathcal{O}(r^{-3})$ near a singularity $s \in S$, and using integration by parts as before we easily deduce that when $m \geq 4$, $\nabla^{g} T$ is $L^1$ and coincides with the covariant derivative computed on $M \setminus S$. This prove that $T$ is covariantly divergence-free on $M$ in the sense of distributions, and hence $\phi$ is stationary.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
